content: The primary goal of asthma management is to enable individuals to take control of their condition. A personalised asthma action plan (PAAP), also referred to as a written action plan, individualised action plan, or self-management action plan, is designed to support this objective. A PAAP provides tailored self-management instructions that are developed collaboratively with the patient. These instructions aim to help maintain asthma control and regain stability during exacerbations. A PAAP typically includes baseline clinical characteristics (e.g., lung function), details of maintenance medications, and specific guidance on how to respond to worsening symptoms and when to seek medical attention. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness of PAAPs, either used alone or in combination with educational interventions, in improving patient-reported outcomes, healthcare resource utilisation, and safety among adults with asthma. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, clinical trial registries, reference lists, and relevant manufacturers' websites up to September 14, 2016. The review included parallel randomised controlled trials (RCTs), both blinded and unblinded, that evaluated written PAAPs in adults with asthma. Comparisons were made between PAAP alone versus no PAAP, and PAAP combined with education versus education alone. Two independent reviewers extracted data on study characteristics and outcomes, and assessed the risk of bias for each included study. The primary outcomes evaluated were the number of participants experiencing at least one exacerbation requiring an emergency department (ED) visit or hospitalisation, asthma symptom scores measured on a validated scale, and adverse events (including all causes). Secondary outcomes included quality of life (measured on a validated scale), the number of participants requiring systemic corticosteroids for exacerbations, respiratory function, and days lost from work or study. A random-effects model was used for all analyses, following standard Cochrane methodology. Fifteen studies, described in 27 articles, met the inclusion criteria, involving a total of 3,062 participants. Of these, 2,602 participants were included in comparisons of PAAP versus no PAAP, and 460 participants were included in comparisons of PAAP plus education versus education alone. Ten studies provided data for quantitative analyses. The overall quality of evidence was rated as low or very low. Fourteen studies had a duration of six months or longer, while one study lasted 14 weeks. The mean age of participants ranged from 22 to 49 years, and asthma severity varied from mild to severe or high-risk. Findings for PAAP Alone Versus No PAAP: There was no clear evidence of benefit or harm in terms of the number of participants requiring an ED visit or hospitalisation for an exacerbation (odds ratio [OR] 0.75, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.45 to 1.24; 1,385 participants; five studies; low-quality evidence). One study reported a small improvement in asthma symptoms (mean difference [MD] -0.16, 95% CI -0.25 to -0.07; 141 participants; low-quality evidence). There was no clear evidence of benefit or harm regarding serious adverse events, including death (OR 3.26, 95% CI 0.33 to 32.21; 125 participants; one study; very low-quality evidence). Quality of life scores showed a statistically significant improvement for those receiving PAAP compared to no PAAP (MD 0.18, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.30; 441 participants; three studies; low-quality evidence), but this improvement did not meet the threshold for a minimum clinically important difference (MCID). There was no clear evidence of benefit or harm in the number of participants requiring oral corticosteroids for exacerbations (OR 1.45, 95% CI 0.84 to 2.48; 1,136 participants; three studies; very low-quality evidence). Respiratory function, measured as change in forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), showed no significant difference (MD -0.04 L, 95% CI -0.25 L to 0.17 L; 392 participants; three studies; low-quality evidence). One study reported significantly fewer days lost from work or study for participants using PAAPs (MD -6.20 days, 95% CI -7.32 to -5.08; 74 participants; low-quality evidence). Findings for PAAP Plus Education Versus Education Alone: There was no clear evidence of benefit or harm in the number of participants requiring an ED visit or hospitalisation for an exacerbation (OR 1.08, 95% CI 0.27 to 4.32; 70 participants; one study; very low-quality evidence). Asthma symptom scores showed no significant difference (MD -0.10, 95% CI -0.54 to 0.34; 70 participants; one study; low-quality evidence). Quality of life scores showed no significant improvement (MD 0.13, 95% CI -0.13 to 0.39; 174 participants; one study; low-quality evidence). There was no clear evidence of benefit or harm in the number of participants requiring oral corticosteroids for exacerbations (OR 0.28, 95% CI 0.07 to 1.12; 70 participants; one study; very low-quality evidence). No studies reported data on serious adverse events, respiratory function, or days lost from work or study. Conclusions: The analysis of available studies was limited by inconsistent reporting of primary and secondary outcomes, making it challenging to draw definitive conclusions about the effectiveness of PAAPs in managing adult asthma. There was no evidence from RCTs to suggest additional benefit or harm associated with PAAPs compared to no PAAP, or PAAPs combined with education compared to education alone. However, the quality of evidence was low or very low, meaning that the reliability of these findings is uncertain. No observable effects were noted on primary outcomes such as hospital attendance for asthma exacerbations, asthma symptom scores, or adverse events. Further research is needed, particularly focusing on key patient-relevant outcomes such as exacerbation frequency and quality of life, and including a broader range of adults, especially those over 60 years of age.
